name: I. Deep Weep
title: I. Deep Weep - Distance (A) and Augmentation (B)
description:
The first movement centres on a feedback loop between a transducer placed on the bass drum skin, a contact microphone, and a mixer. My question was how to make the relationships—which in the original score remain largely invisible— between these objects perceptible to an audience. I pursued two directions.

In the first (A), I introduced long aluminium poles as extensions of my body, positioning the instruments at a significant distance from one another and from myself. A two-metre pole connects me to the bass drum; another carries a cello bow for playing the thunder sheet; a third, fitted with a caliber, operates the mixer's sliders. The transducer itself is mounted partway along the pole rather than directly on the skin, so that the feedback loop runs through the metal of the pole—adding a further layer of mediation.

In the second version (B), I kept the spatial arrangement closer to the original but replaced the instruments with larger counterparts—an 18” crash instead of a 10” splash cymbal, a bass drum microphone instead of a contact microphone, a larger cone transducer. This changed the conditions under which feedback persists in ways I had not fully anticipated: the larger microphone continues to pick up residual sound even when the transducer is lifted away from the skin, so that the movement of raising and lowering the cone becomes a significant gestural and sonic event in itself. I found myself dwelling in those moments, taking more time than the score strictly indicates.

name: II. E-Guitars
title: II- E-Guitars - On an Inhabited Planet
description:
The second movement has a dialogic structure built into the score: two staves, one for each transducer, with performance indications—lullaby, singing, speaking, heated discussion—that suggest something closer to a conversation than a musical texture. During an improvisation session, I filmed myself, and a particular camera angle—frontal, close to the bass drum, tight on the skin—made the drum surface look like a stage and the two transducers like figures inhabiting a small, circular world. From that point, the process moved in the direction of puppet theatre. I developed a fictional world in considerable detail. The two transducers became characters— Dr. Melian Pirek, an experienced researcher, methodical and somewhat irritable, and Skael Urden, younger, impulsive, full of nervous energy—stranded together on an uninhabited planet after a crash. The fermata signs and short breaks in the score became scene divisions; the performance indications became relational attitudes between two interlocutors. I identified seven scenes, each with its own dramatic character, tracing an arc from a first encounter and an attempt at collaboration, through teaching, private brooding, conflict and estrangement, to a final fragile togetherness. The sounds produced by the transducers shift register depending on the dramatic context— sometimes functioning as the characters' research methods, sometimes as their language, sometimes as expressions of emotional states. The transducers do not speak in human language; instead, I use my own voice as an external narrator, giving the story a frame across the different scenes, alongside visual intertitles—scene numbers and temporal indications appearing on a black screen between scenes.

Plot

Scene 1: Meeting
Two researchers, Urden and Dr. Pirek, enter the space from opposite sides. Their first encounter is tentative: surprise, hesitation, curiosity, and a cautious greeting. They approach the cymbals that form their research field, but while Dr. Pirek begins his work with calm assurance, Urden struggles to produce the elusive "H" sound and conceals his uncertainty behind a stream of questions.

Scene 2: Teaching
Recognising Urden's frustration, Dr. Pirek steps away from his own work to share his experience. He demonstrates a simple sequence—breath, approach, touch, pressure, release—and patiently encourages Urden to try. Despite moments of progress, success remains inconsistent, and encouragement gives way to quiet frustration.

Scene 3: Nostalgic Song
Time passes. Urden continues to practise obsessively while Dr. Pirek withdraws into an evening ritual before singing a nostalgic melody. Effortlessly, and almost absent-mindedly, the song ends with the very sound Urden has been chasing, bringing his practice to an abrupt halt.

Scene 4: Loud Music
Several days later, the two have settled into a shared routine. Their contrasting working habits begin to clash: Dr. Pirek seeks silence and concentration, while Urden relies on loud music to remain focused and avoid loneliness. A disagreement escalates into an animated argument about methods, priorities, and authority, ending in an unresolved confrontation.

Scene 5: Conflict
The conflict leaves both researchers withdrawn. They return to work from opposite sides of the space, their movements subdued and their attention divided between the research and each other.

Scene 6: Brooding, Murmuring
In its aftermath, they retreat to opposite sides of the space. They return to their work separately, murmuring to themselves, absorbed in their own frustrations and unable to hear the other. Gradually, their complaints soften into attentive listening. Brief glances replace avoidance, revealing that they are struggling with the same difficulties.

Scene 7: Togetherness
Slowly they move toward one another. Working side by side, they recognise a shared persistence rather than their differences. When Urden finally produces the "H" sound, both react with surprise and delight. The work closes with a moment of closeness, celebration, and shared discovery.

name: III. Mouth - S
title: III. Mouth - S
description: The third movement follows a similar interpretive direction to the first—feedback understood as a network of relationships—but pursues it differently. Rather than making relationships visible from the outside, I became interested in the possibility of collapsing the distance between listener and network entirely. My interpretation took the form of an interactive installation. A thunder sheet—one of the same thunder sheets used in my recordings of the piece—hangs from a stand, with a transducer attached to its surface playing back my recording of the movement at a deliberately low volume. The sound does not project strongly into the air, but it sets the metal itself into vibration, transforming the object into a resonant surface. The audience is given a stethoscope and invited to press it against the surface at different points, discovering that the sheet does not sound the same everywhere—that it has its own acoustic geography, and that listening from within the vibration is a different experience from listening to it from outside. During the development I also experimented with teeth conduction—transmitting vibration through a wooden or glass object held between the teeth—and with a Pinard horn, the wooden instrument traditionally used by midwives to listen to a foetal heartbeat. Both offered compelling modes of contact but raised practical concerns: the need for higher playback volumes, hygiene issues with shared objects, and the risk that too many tools would turn the installation into a demonstration of techniques rather than keeping the encounter between audience and surface itself at the centre.

name: IV. Out of Breath
title: IV. Out of Breath - I Don't Know What to Do, Therefore I Scream!
description: The fourth movement was the last I developed, and the most difficult. Going back to the score several times, I paid much closer attention to its paratext: the title—Out of Breath / Tired After Run, Catching the Breath—the tempo marking (scream-breathe, natural, bodily flow), the performance indications (angry, very high energy; last energy hype; exhausted but keep tension; calming completely down; tired; into absolute stillness). The question that emerged was whether to take those indications more literally—not only as sonic metaphors but as actual physical and emotional conditions to inhabit. This brought me back to a conversation with Pranulytė from nearly two years earlier, in which she described how the piece was built around an analogy between percussion instruments and the vocal apparatus—the way certain techniques, like folding the thunder sheet, change resonance in ways that approximate the filtering behaviour of a mouth, without the instrument ever becoming a voice. Breath was central to this: she spoke about finding ways to let the sound, the space, the intensity, and the dramaturgy breathe. I therefore began developing a version in which I use my voice—screaming and breathing—as the primary sound source, pressing my mouth against the metal surfaces so that the voice is filtered by the material rather than projected into the room. I set the bow aside: listening back to recordings I had made with a contact microphone on the metal surfaces, I found that the contact microphone track evoked enough of the sonic character of the bow to stand in for it. The screaming, filtered through the metal plate behind which I am not visible to the audience, loses some of its more extreme extra-musical associations—with pain, violence, distress—without losing its physical intensity. A pre-recorded vocal layer, made by singing into a tam-tam through a contact microphone, fills in the humming and vowel sounds that the score calls for but that I can no longer perform simultaneously with the screaming.
